title: Palestine is already living under the Big Tech authoritarianism the world is being sold
content:
Emerging technologies have become central to systems of coercion and control

Originally published on Global Voices Advox

An aerial view showing destruction in Rafah, Gaza Strip, on January 21, 2025. Photo by Ashraf Amra on Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO).

By Jalal Abukhater

This post is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.

For Palestinians, the relationship between technology and authoritarianism is a lived reality, rather than predictions or science fiction. Israel’s settler-colonial regime has long fused military force with legal, economic and technological mechanisms to dominate Palestinian life.
snippet:
Emerging technologies have become central to systems of coercion and control

title: When Big Tech becomes a tool of state control in Kenya
content:
State censorship on information has moved from broadcasters to platforms and the laws that govern them

Originally published on Global Voices Advox

Image of person using Telegram by Christian Wiediger via Unsplash (Free to use). Image of Kenyan flag by User:Pumbaa80 via Wikimedia Commons(Public domain). Illustration by Global Voices.

This post by Grace Kobare is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.

On January 30, 2018, Raila Odinga held his symbolic “swearing-in” ceremony in Nairobi, and the government, through Kenya’s regulator, switched off the transmitters of KTN, NTV and Citizen TV while they were broadcasting live.

The Interior Ministry defended the move, saying the media had been given a security briefing in advance. The stations stayed off air for days and were only fully back by February 9, 2018.
snippet:
State censorship on information has moved from broadcasters to platforms and the laws that govern them

title: Anthropic exposes AI operation that DRC journalists never knew existed
content:
Disinformation surrounding DRC-Rwanda relations has weakened the diplomatic and public standing of both countries

Originally published on Global Voices Advox

Featured image from DRC media, created using screenshots from ACP's YouTube channel

This post is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.

In September 2026, Anthropic, an artificial intelligence (AI) development and research company, exposed a network of fake news sites targeting the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). The investigation revealed that large-scale, AI-powered disinformation campaigns have emerged at a time of conflict when trust in the news is already at an all-time low and resources are severely limited.

title: How an extremist network articulated a hoax linking Brazil’s President Lula to child abuse on X
content:
Monitoring of 1,819 posts showed far-right users tried to manipulate Grok, X’s AI tool

Originally published on Global Voices Advox

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Art by: Méuri Elle/Aos Fatos, used with permission.

This article was originally published on the fact-checking agency Aos Fatos website, on September 30, 2026. It is part of the joint initiative Laboratório de Investigação Eleitoral (Investigative Electoral Lab) with Agência Pública, Amado Mundo and Núcleo Jornalismo. An edited version is republished here under a partnership agreement between Global Voices and Pública.

A few days before the first round of the 2026 general elections in Brazil on October 4, it took only a few hours for a line said by President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva about preventive exams for prostate cancer to be twisted into a pedophilia accusation against him. Aos Fatos obtained and checked 1,819 posts on X (formerly Twitter), which reconstructed how this hoax was planted and harvested by Bolsonarista users on social media between September 28 and 29.
snippet:
Monitoring of 1,819 posts showed far-right users tried to manipulate Grok, X’s AI tool

title: Hong Kong police launch AI-powered national security platform for school pupils
content:
‘May the seeds of national security take root and sprout in the hearts of the pupils…’

Originally published on Global Voices Advox

Hong Kong police launch an AI-powered national security education platform for the city’s pupils during a ceremony on October 6, 2026. Photo: HKPF, via Facebook. Used with permission.

This article was originally published by Hong Kong Free Press on October 13, 2026. The following version is republished on Global Voices under a content partnership agreement. It is also part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” You can support this coverage by donating here.

Hong Kong police have launched an artificial intelligence-powered national security education platform for young students.

The NSmarties AI Interactive Platform was officially launched on October 6, 2026, at a ceremony at Precious Blood Primary School in Ap Lei Chau, with about 700 pupils attending, police said in a Facebook post:

【 NSmarties童心護港AI互動平台 • 正式啟動 】
國家安全，由童心出發！
由警務處國家安全處主辦的「NSmarties童心護港AI互動平台」今日（6日）於海怡寶血小學正式啟動！ 警務處處長周一鳴、警務處副處長（國家安全）江學禮、寶血會總會長區綺雯修女等一眾嘉賓，聯同約700位同學一同見證這個重要時刻。
啟動禮圓滿結束，標誌着國安教育以創新科技走進校園的新里程！ 願國安種子在同學心裏生根發芽，茁壯成長！
snippet:
‘May the seeds of national security take root and sprout in the hearts of the pupils…’

title: How authoritarian states are building an international market for digital surveillance
content:
The main danger of AI in authoritarian regimes is the ability to suppress any protest

Originally published on Global Voices Advox

Moscow subway cameras are connected to a facial recognition system. Screenshot taken from the YouTube video “Facial recognition cameras help detain dissidents in the Moscow metro” by the DW YouTube channel; fair use.

This post is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Sonya, from Stavropol Krai, Russia, is 15 years old. In June 2026, she was sentenced to 70 hours of compulsory labor, connected to a February 2026 incident in which she had written the surname “Navalny” on a bus stop. That stop happened to be in a district that was being monitored by officers from the Center for Combating Extremism, commonly called Center E. Similarly, Yuri, a pensioner from Astrakhan who was also identified from surveillance footage, was given three years of restricted freedom for writing “No to War” in red marker on buildings.
snippet:
The main danger of AI in authoritarian regimes is the ability to suppress any protest

title: Norway’s Telenor telecom faces lawsuit for giving user data to Myanmar junta
content:
The state-owned company is accused of abetting crimes against humanity

Originally published on Global Voices Advox

Telenor telecom operated in Myanmar from 2014 to 2022. Photo by Bjoertvedt. Source: Wikipedia. CC BY-SA 4.0

This post is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.

The Norway-based multinational telecom company Telenor is facing charges for its role in turning over sensitive customer data to the military government of Myanmar.

If successful, the case would be the first ever to hold a telecom company accountable for failing to protect user data from being misused by an authoritarian regime.
snippet:
The state-owned company is accused of abetting crimes against humanity

title: When free speech has a price: Youth voices in Mozambique
content:
When speaking freely can have a cost, young people turn to music to challenge political silence

Originally published on Global Voices Advox

A group of men during a peaceful protest; one of them holds a microphone and a banner. Photo taken by Stephanie Douglas. Nigeria. Via Pexels. Pexels License.

In Mozambique, freedom of expression is regulated by the Law on the Right to Information No. 34/2014, a constitutionally guaranteed right under Article 48 of the Constitution of the Republic of Mozambique. However, for many young people, speaking publicly about corruption, inequality, police violence, or accountability continues to carry risk, showing the gap between the promises of democracy and actual daily experience.
snippet:
When speaking freely can have a cost, young people turn to music to challenge political silence

title: Trump’s ‘Agreements on Reciprocal Trade’ (ARTs) threaten equitable access to the internet in Global South
content:
The provision could give the U.S. the power to exclude Chinese ICT suppliers in signatory countries

Originally published on Global Voices Advox

Image remix on Canva by Ihsan Kamil/EngageMedia. Used with permission.

This article, written by Rishab Bailey and Prapasiri “Nan” Suttisome, was published by Public Citizen and EngageMedia, a non-profit media, technology, and culture organization, and an edited version is republished here as part of a content-sharing agreement. It is also part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” You can support this coverage by donating here.

Around the world, one in every three people has no reliable access to the internet. Unequal access to the internet creates digital divides that can limit civic participation, undermine access to education and healthcare, and deepen inequality. It can also reduce innovation, industrial growth, and economic output. Reducing digital divides is recognized as essential for progress on the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals, as reaffirmed by the more recent Global Digital Compact, 2024.
snippet:
The provision could give the U.S. the power to exclude Chinese ICT suppliers in signatory countries
